title: Text organization: reader expectations, conversational maxims and the pyramid rules

criteria.name: Follow a grammatical subject as soon as possible with its verb.

definition.text: 1. Follow a grammatical subject as soon as possible with its verb.
definition.locator: American Scientist 78(6), 1990, final section 'Writing and the Scientific Process', numbered list of structural principles, item 1 (Wayback 2021-01-15 copy of the americanscientist.org page)

criteria.condition: None of these reader-expectation principles should be considered "rules." [...] any reader expectation can be violated to good effect.
criteria.example_notes: a19 (hydrogen-bond paragraph, original vs. the authors' final revision): the authors' first revision tactic for this paragraph is to invert the first sentence so the subject-verb-complement connection is unbroken. The final revision also adds two sentences of content.

criteria.name: Place in the stress position the "new information" you want the reader to emphasize.

definition.text: 2. Place in the stress position the "new information" you want the reader to emphasize.
definition.locator: American Scientist 78(6), 1990, final section 'Writing and the Scientific Process', numbered list of structural principles, item 2 (Wayback 2021-01-15 copy of the americanscientist.org page)

criteria.condition: None of these reader-expectation principles should be considered "rules." [...] any reader expectation can be violated to good effect.
criteria.example_notes: a18 (earthquake paragraph): the authors revise it by ensuring, for each sentence, that the new, emphasis-worthy information appears in the stress position. a19: their revision tactics create a stress position for 'triisopropylsilyl groups' and use 'both' to flag two effects in one stress position.

criteria.name: Place the person or thing whose "story" a sentence is telling at the beginning of the sentence, in the topic position.

definition.text: 3. Place the person or thing whose "story" a sentence is telling at the beginning of the sentence, in the topic position.
definition.locator: American Scientist 78(6), 1990, final section 'Writing and the Scientific Process', numbered list of structural principles, item 3 (Wayback 2021-01-15 copy of the americanscientist.org page)

criteria.condition: None of these reader-expectation principles should be considered "rules." [...] any reader expectation can be violated to good effect.
criteria.example_notes: a18: the authors' second revision condition is that the person, thing or concept whose story it is appears in the topic position. a19: the authors note that in the original 'we are not sure at all times whose story is being told'.

criteria.name: Place appropriate "old information" (material already stated in the discourse) in the topic position for linkage backward and contextualization forward.

definition.text: 4. Place appropriate "old information" (material already stated in the discourse) in the topic position for linkage backward and contextualization forward.
definition.locator: American Scientist 78(6), 1990, final section 'Writing and the Scientific Process', numbered list of structural principles, item 4 (Wayback 2021-01-15 copy of the americanscientist.org page)

criteria.condition: None of these reader-expectation principles should be considered "rules." [...] any reader expectation can be violated to good effect.
criteria.example_notes: a18: the authors' first revision condition is that the backward-linking old information appears in the topic position. a19: introduced as the example showing that when old information does not appear at all, readers are left to construct the logical linkage; the final revision supplies the missing linking sentences.

criteria.name: Articulate the action of every clause or sentence in its verb.

definition.text: 5. Articulate the action of every clause or sentence in its verb.
definition.locator: American Scientist 78(6), 1990, final section 'Writing and the Scientific Process', numbered list of structural principles, item 5 (Wayback 2021-01-15 copy of the americanscientist.org page)

criteria.name: every unit of discourse, no matter the size, should serve a single function or make a single point

definition.text: We now have three rhetorical principles based on reader expectations: [...] second, every unit of discourse, no matter the size, should serve a single function or make a single point;
definition.locator: Section 'The Stress Position', summary of the three rhetorical principles (the second is not repeated in the final numbered list)

criteria.name: The Cooperative Principle

definition.text: Make your conversational contribution such as is required, at the stage at which it occurs, by the accepted purpose or direction of the talk exchange in which you are engaged.
definition.locator: Grice 1975 'Logic and Conversation' (Grice 1989, pp. 26-27 as cited by SEP); original not seen. Wording verified against: SEP 'Paul Grice' §3 'Conversational implicature' and the MIT OCW 24.903 handout 'Grice's System'

criteria.condition: at the stage at which it occurs, by the accepted purpose or direction of the talk exchange in which you are engaged

criteria.name: Quantity 1

definition.text: Make your contribution as informative as is required [...] (for the current purposes of the exchange).
definition.locator: Grice 1975 'Logic and Conversation' (Grice 1989, pp. 26-27 as cited by SEP); original not seen. Wording verified against: MIT OCW handout (maxim text); the parenthetical is absent from that handout and is verified against Tanswell (Aporia, St Andrews) and Garnock-Jones (2017 thesis, arXiv 2409.04055), both quoting Grice 1975

criteria.condition: (for the current purposes of the exchange)

criteria.name: Quantity 2

definition.text: Do not make your contribution more informative than is required.
definition.locator: Grice 1975 'Logic and Conversation' (Grice 1989, pp. 26-27 as cited by SEP); original not seen. Wording verified against: MIT OCW handout

criteria.name: Quality (supermaxim)

definition.text: Try to make your contribution one that is true
definition.locator: Grice 1975 'Logic and Conversation' (Grice 1989, pp. 26-27 as cited by SEP); original not seen. Wording verified against: SEP 'Paul Grice' §3

criteria.name: Quality 1

definition.text: Do not say what you believe to be false.
definition.locator: Grice 1975 'Logic and Conversation' (Grice 1989, pp. 26-27 as cited by SEP); original not seen. Wording verified against: MIT OCW handout

criteria.name: Quality 2

definition.text: Do not say that for which you lack adequate evidence.
definition.locator: Grice 1975 'Logic and Conversation' (Grice 1989, pp. 26-27 as cited by SEP); original not seen. Wording verified against: MIT OCW handout

criteria.name: Relation

definition.text: Be relevant.
definition.locator: Grice 1975 'Logic and Conversation' (Grice 1989, pp. 26-27 as cited by SEP); original not seen. Wording verified against: SEP 'Paul Grice' §3 and MIT OCW handout

criteria.name: Manner (supermaxim)

definition.text: Be perspicuous
definition.locator: Grice 1975 'Logic and Conversation' (Grice 1989, pp. 26-27 as cited by SEP); original not seen. Wording verified against: SEP 'Paul Grice' §3

criteria.name: Manner 1

definition.text: Avoid obscurity of expression.
definition.locator: Grice 1975 'Logic and Conversation' (Grice 1989, pp. 26-27 as cited by SEP); original not seen. Wording verified against: MIT OCW handout

criteria.name: Manner 2

definition.text: Avoid ambiguity.
definition.locator: Grice 1975 'Logic and Conversation' (Grice 1989, pp. 26-27 as cited by SEP); original not seen. Wording verified against: MIT OCW handout

criteria.name: Manner 3

definition.text: Be brief (avoid unnecessary prolixity).
definition.locator: Grice 1975 'Logic and Conversation' (Grice 1989, pp. 26-27 as cited by SEP); original not seen. Wording verified against: MIT OCW handout ('Be brief.'); the parenthetical is verified against Tanswell (Aporia) and Garnock-Jones (arXiv 2409.04055)

criteria.name: Manner 4

definition.text: Be orderly.
definition.locator: Grice 1975 'Logic and Conversation' (Grice 1989, pp. 26-27 as cited by SEP); original not seen. Wording verified against: MIT OCW handout

criteria.name: present their information from the top down

definition.text: the clearest written documents will be those that consistently present their information from the top down, in a pyramidal structure, even though the original thinking will have been done from the bottom up.
definition.locator: Minto, The Minto Pyramid Principle ([1996] 2018), ch. 1, p. 7, as quoted with page reference by manager138.com notes; book not seen

criteria.name: Ideas at any level in the pyramid must always be summaries of the ideas grouped below them

definition.text: Ideas at any level in the pyramid must always be summaries of the ideas grouped below them.
definition.locator: Minto, The Minto Pyramid Principle ([1996] 2018), ch. 1 'Pyramid rules', p. 9, as quoted with page reference by manager138.com notes; book not seen; same wording quoted by strategyu.co and ConsultingMethodology.com

criteria.name: Ideas in each grouping must always be the same kind of idea

definition.text: Ideas in each grouping must always be the same kind of idea. [...] Be sure you can label the ideas with a plural noun.
definition.locator: Minto, The Minto Pyramid Principle ([1996] 2018), ch. 1 'Pyramid rules', pp. 9-10, as quoted with page reference by manager138.com notes; book not seen; rule wording also quoted by strategyu.co

criteria.name: Ideas in each grouping must always be logically ordered

definition.text: Ideas in each grouping must always be logically ordered. [...] Deductively (major premise, minor premise, conclusion) Chronologically (first, second, third) Structurally (Boston, New York, Washington) Comparatively (first most important, second most important, etc)
definition.locator: Minto, The Minto Pyramid Principle ([1996] 2018), ch. 1 'Pyramid rules', pp. 9-11, as quoted with page reference by manager138.com notes; book not seen; rule wording also quoted by strategyu.co and ConsultingMethodology.com
